What a roller coaster! Following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, markets initially plunged overnight, with S&P 500 $SPX futures down nearly 100 handles.

But by morning, futures had staged a massive reversal, with $SPY indicated $8 higher and $QQQ up roughly $3.

Is this the beginning of a sustainable post-election rally into Christmas, or just another bull trap?

*

The most important thing right now is to focus on what we can control: risk management, price action, and making good trading decisions rather than getting caught up in political headlines.

Here's what REALLY matters:

1. $SPY: a potential double bottom and a bullish gap pivot?

$SPY has tested the $749–750 area twice, potentially establishing a double bottom.

Now we're seeing a powerful gap higher, with #SPY approaching $763. The key is whether buyers can defend today's gains.

Holding $763 and, more importantly, $757 could create a bullish gap pivot and open the door to a move toward the upper end of the trading range.

But if we lose $763, break below $757, and print another big red candle, this rally could quickly turn into another failed breakout.

2.  $QQQ: reclaiming the 200-day moving average!

Technology has been relatively weak, but $QQQ is now back above its 200-day moving average, with $698 an important level to watch.

Sometimes markets test the 200-day, experience distribution, and then reclaim it. If that reclaim holds, it could signal a meaningful improvement in the trend.

*

Some thoughts on $TSLA & $SPCX after Democrats win.

First of all, #Tesla was one of the weakest names yesterday, and its bearish-looking candle prompted me to exit my position ahead of the election results. That decision saved me from today's roughly $18 premarket decline.

With concerns that Democrats could target Elon Musk, #TSLA is under pressure.

However, the 200-day moving average and a nearby gap fill around $377 could provide support.

I'll be watching whether Tesla establishes a five-minute low and bounces before considering a tactical entry.

$SPCX on the other hand hasn't been acting well for active swing traders.

If the election turns out to be a clearing event and the market rallies into Thanksgiving and Christmas, Amazon could be one of the names worth holding.

So, the bigger question now: can we finally get a sustainable two-to-six-week trend instead of another frustrating one-day bounce?

I'd love to see a market where we can build positions, hold winners, and get paid for sitting in them. But I'm not chasing this massive gap higher. I'm actually trimming some exposure into strength and watching how much of the opening move holds.

The next few sessions will tell us whether this is the start of a real year-end rally or just another opportunity to sell into strength.

posts.text:
Yesterday we highlighted that the volatility market was pricing a small potential move in the S&P 500. The index ended up 1.6% on Nov 4th, well beyond the 1.2% move implied by the volatility market.

The Momentum factor* fell more than 6%, placing in the bottom 1% of all daily returns in at least a decade. Prior winners fell almost as much as prior losers rallied. Semiconductors fell below July lows while Consumer Discretionary outperformed Energy by over 9%.

Remarkably, the Beta factor* is down almost 3% despite the sharp rally in equities. This comes on the back of its worst month in 15 years, with Beta falling 22% in October.

YTD stats are striking. Beta is down 11% and Momentum 14%, while the S&P 500 is up 12%.

The simultaneous selloff in Beta and Momentum has echoes of July, but the drivers are different.

July was the worst month for Momentum in 15 years, driven by a positioning unwind as investors sold prior winners. October was the worst month for Beta in 15 years, driven by a broader macro shock as tightening financial conditions punished high-volatility stocks.

* Morgan Stanley Institutional Equity Division is measuring Momentum here as the performance difference between the top 200 outperformers vs. the bottom 200 underperformers of the Russell 3000 over the past 12 months with a 1-month lag. Beta is measured as the performance difference between the top 15% of liquid Russell 3000 members based on 6 and 24-month betas and the bottom 15% on the same metric.

He cares about ideas and whether they are right or wrong, and he would rather lose every election in his lifetime doing the right thing than win a single one doing the wrong thing. He holds a standard, measures his actions against it, and knows before the returns come in whether he governed by it. When men abandon reason as their guide, the opinion survey becomes their substitute for thought.

Not one word about roughly 30 government equity stakes in private companies, which is socialism practiced by the party that claims to oppose it. The midterm election delivered a considerably stronger Democratic showing than the market was anticipating. Democrats captured both the House and Senate, with gains extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds and into states and districts that had been reliably Republican. The result is a genuine blue wave and, from the market's perspective, the important issue this morning isn't politics -- it's surprise. Markets can discount good news and bad news; what they have a more difficult time discounting is an outcome that wasn't fully anticipated.

Historically, that reduction in legislative flexibility has not necessarily been a negative for stocks. Markets generally prefer predictability, and divided government can make sweeping changes in taxes, spending and regulation more difficult to enact. Fidelity's research makes an important point: historically, the market's post-election behavior has been driven less by which political party won than by the reduction in uncertainty once the election was over. As Fidelity puts it, the environment doesn't necessarily become completely clear - it simply becomes “less unclear.” And this is where the historical picture becomes particularly interesting.

Since 1938, the S&P 500 has been higher 95% of the time during the 12 months following a midterm election, with an average gain of approximately 14%. Fidelity's longer-term work on the presidential cycle also shows the post-midterm year as historically the strongest portion of the four-year election cycle. Schwab finds a similar pattern: since 1974, the S&P 500 has averaged a 5.7% gain in the three months following midterms and 12.4% over the following six months.

That historical tendency is reinforced by seasonality. We have now entered what has traditionally been the strongest six-month period of the year, November through April. Since 1945, the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 7% during that six-month stretch versus just over 2% from May through October. November itself has historically been one of the market's strongest months, and the November through January period has also been particularly favorable

So we now have several potentially favorable historical forces beginning to converge: the election is behind us, political uncertainty has been reduced, Washington is moving toward divided government, we're entering the historically strongest part of the presidential cycle, and we're simultaneously moving into one of the strongest seasonal periods of the year.

That does not mean the market has to go straight up from here. In fact, given the magnitude of the election surprise, some additional volatility would not be unusual. The market still has to digest what the Democratic Congress could mean for taxes, regulation, AI infrastructure, energy policy and other areas. More importantly, the election doesn't make the other risks disappear. The 10-year Treasury yield remains near 5%, oil remains above $100, inflation and Fed policy remain significant issues, and questions surrounding AI valuations and capital spending are still very much in play. Those fundamental forces ultimately matter more than the election itself.

What matters now is whether the tape begins to confirm the historical script. I want to see the major indexes absorb the election shock and hold support, but even more important, I want to see improvement beneath the surface: broader participation, expanding leadership, more stocks reclaiming key moving averages, fewer new lows, more quality setups and, ultimately, breakouts that can gain traction and hold their gains.

Dat is wat iemand die 100.000 euro op een spaarrekening bij de grootbanken had gezet sinds 2020 aan koopkracht heeft verloren. 20% van je koopkracht zomaar verdwenen.

De reden is simpel. In Nederland is de rente zo laag dat je met ‘veilig’ sparen niet eens in de buurt komt van het tempo waarmee het dagelijkse leven elk jaar duurder wordt.

Sinds 2020 ligt de inflatie gemiddeld op net geen 4% (3,9% om precies te zijn). Schrik niet: volgens De Nederlandsche Bank lag de spaarrente over dezelfde periode op 0,7%. Geen wonder dat de koopkracht van ons spaargeld zo extreem hard is gedaald.

Zelfs als je bij andere banken gemiddeld een procentpunt meer rente had gekregen, is de koopkracht van die 100.000 euro sinds 2020 nog steeds met meer dan 15% gedaald.

Ik neem die 100.000 euro omdat dit het maximale bedrag is dat, op papier, per persoon, per bank wordt beschermd via het depositogarantiestelsel. Daar zit naar schatting nu zo’n 5 miljard euro in. Dat bedrag kan, wederom op papier, worden vergroot. Mocht zich een systeemcrisis voordoen, waarbij meerdere banken omvallen, dan is de kans groot dat slechts een deel van die 100.000 euro wordt vergoed.

Immers, het totale Nederlandse spaargeld bedraagt momenteel liefst 666 miljard euro (een ironisch getal). Mijn schatting is dat de koopkracht van al het Nederlandse spaargeld sinds 2020 met grofweg 100 miljard euro is afgenomen.

Laat dat even rustig op je inwerken. En weet je wat het bizarre is? Zelfs als maar de helft van ons spaargeld (je hebt nu eenmaal een potje nodig voor als het even tegenzit) de voorbije jaren slim was belegd, dan zaten Nederlanders er nog een heel, heel stuk warmer bij.
